source_refs.note: Topic 8.2 with the class activity (PDF 198-199, printed 195-196). The book names types of research questions and hypotheses but never explains them, though short questions 3 and 4 ask about them; answered from general knowledge, flagged. MCQ 4 (b) matches the key. Recorded.

blocks.text: Formulating research inquiries means creating the questions that guide research and keep it focused on what you want to learn. A well-thought-out question is the first step of a successful project and sets the direction of the whole study (Did You Know).

The book says there are different types of research questions but does not list them; the following is general knowledge. An exploratory question investigates a little-understood topic to discover what is going on (What study habits do Class XI students have?). An explanatory question asks why or how something happens, looking for causes (Why do students who sleep more get better marks?). A hypothesis is a testable prediction based on a question (Students who sleep at least eight hours score higher than those who sleep less); it guides what data to collect and can be supported or rejected by evidence.

Bottom left: five research-ethics principles with one-line meanings. Bottom right: a table of patent, trademark, copyright, industrial design and trade secret with what each protects and the book's example.
blocks.caption: Research steps, research ethics and intellectual property (original diagram after topics 8.2 to 8.5).
blocks.long_description: A research project moves from a clear question to a testable hypothesis, then to finding sources in libraries and databases, judging them (for example whether they are peer-reviewed), organizing notes and files, and reporting findings with every source cited. Ethical research asks participants' informed consent, keeps their answers confidential, never fakes data or plagiarizes, avoids harm and lets evidence, not bias, decide. Intellectual property protects inventions with patents, brands with trademarks, creative works with copyright, product looks with industrial designs and confidential know-how as trade secrets.

blocks.prompt: Why be specific when formulating a research question (MCQ 4)? Differentiate exploratory and explanatory questions (short question 3). Why is a hypothesis important (short question 4)?
blocks.explanation: (b) to define clearly what you want to find out and avoid vague questions. Exploratory questions explore a new or unclear topic to describe it; explanatory questions seek the causes or reasons behind something. A hypothesis turns the question into a testable prediction, focusing what data to collect and giving a clear way to judge the results.

blocks.prompt: Explain how to develop a clear, focused research question, with well- and poorly-formulated examples (long question 3). Class activity: write a question and hypothesis on a topic you are curious about.
blocks.explanation: Start with a broad topic, narrow it to one aspect, name who or what is studied, the variables and the setting, and make sure it can be answered with available data. Poor: 'Is social media bad?' (vague and too broad). Good: 'Does daily social-media use of more than two hours lower the weekly study time of Class XI students in our college?' A matching hypothesis: 'Students who use social media more than two hours a day study fewer hours per week.' The examples are general knowledge.

items: Good research questions are clear and specific; a hypothesis is a testable prediction; exploratory describes, explanatory explains.
